わたし が すき な ひと — The person I love
You describe people and things with whole clauses placed before the noun (“the book THAT I bought”) and say when something happens (～とき).
This is the book I bought yesterday.
Who is the person with glasses?
The food I like is sushi.
When I was a child, I often went to the seaside.
When I have free time, I play the guitar.
To put a whole clause before a noun: きのう かった ほん (the book I bought yesterday).
To use が (not は) inside these clauses: わたし が すき な ひと.
To describe people by what they do or wear: めがね を かけて いる ひと.
To say when something happens: ～とき (こども の とき, ひま な とき, いく とき).
To choose a present with the help of a shop assistant.
The last day in Hiroshima. Ana has gone to Miyajima with Sakura. Mihai has asked Haruka to come with him to a jeweller’s. He has a secret plan.
Welcome. What are you looking for?
Er… I’m looking for a ring. A ring I want to give to someone special.
Not yet! I haven’t asked her yet…
Hee-hee. Mihai, what’s Ana’s favourite colour?
Blue. She said she likes a blue like the sea in Spain.
Then how about this one? It’s a silver ring with a blue stone.
It’s beautiful… But I think it’s a bit big. Because Ana likes small things.
Then I think this one would be better. It’s a ring inspired by the Seto Inland Sea.
Ah, it’s the same colour as the sea Ana was looking at yesterday, at Miyajima.
I’ll take this one! …And the size, what do I do…
No problem. I think it’s the same size as my ring that Ana wore yesterday.
What, Haruka…! Did you know from the start?
Anyone could tell, seeing the way you look at Ana.
Shall I put it in a heart-shaped box?
No… an ordinary box, please. It’s a secret!
“osagashi desu ka” = are you looking for? (polite)
“to itte imashita” = said that; with (compared with)
yu-bi-wa: three equal syllables. わ is “wa”, not “ua”.
An onomatopoeia for a pounding heart: do-ki-do-ki. Japanese has hundreds of words like this!
o-me-de-toh go-za-i-mas: a long o in “toh”. It’s the congratulation for anything: birthday, engagement, new year.
1. The clause comes BEFORE the noun

In English we say “the book THAT I bought yesterday”: the noun comes first, the description after, with “that”. In Japanese it’s the reverse: the whole description comes BEFORE, in the casual form, with no “that”:
It’s exactly how adjectives work! あたらしい ほん (a new book) → きのう かった ほん (a book bought yesterday). The whole clause behaves like one big adjective.
Inside it’s always the CASUAL form: “かいました ほん” is wrong; the correct form is かった ほん.
The subject inside the descriptive clause is marked with が (or の), NEVER with は:
わたし が つくった ケーキ (the cake I made)
アナさん が すき な いろ (the colour Ana likes)
The cake I made is tasty.
は shows the topic of the BIG sentence (ケーキ は おいしい). が shows the subject of the SMALL clause inside (わたし が つくった).
Watch out for な adjectives: すき な いろ (with な), as in chapter 7. And nouns: いしゃ の ひと / いしゃ だった ひと.
This is how you describe people by what they wear or do. Very useful when you don’t know someone’s name:
the person with glasses (who is wearing glasses)
the person playing the guitar over there
Each item of clothing has its own verb: きる (clothes on the body), はく (trousers, shoes), かぶる (hat), かける (glasses), つける (jewellery).
とき (the moment) behaves like a noun. You describe it exactly as in point 1:
こども の とき (when I was a child)
ひま な とき (when I have free time)
さむい とき (when it’s cold)
にほん へ いく とき (when I go to Japan)
When I feel lonely, I call my mother.
An advanced nuance: いく とき = when I go / on the way (not yet arrived). いった とき = when I got there. にほん へ いった とき、カメラ を かいました = I bought the camera when I went to Japan (there).
5. Giving and receiving: あげます / もらいます
I は YOU に X を あげます
I は YOU に/から X を もらいます
There’s also くれます (someone gives ME something). You’ve seen it in the stories: たすけて くれました. You’ll learn it systematically at N4.
This is the watch I got from my father for my birthday.
This is the film I saw yesterday.

ことば に できない きもち — What can’t be put into words
At the bottom of his bag there was a little box. The ring he had bought that day.
“I wonder when I should give it to her…”
Mihai took out his notebook and began to write. To note down what he wanted to say to Ana.
At first he wrote in Spanish. But the words wouldn’t come.
Then he wrote in Romanian. It was easier, but Ana doesn’t understand Romanian.
Finally, he tried writing in Japanese.
“When we first met, you were the Spanish teacher.”
“You always patiently explained the words I didn’t understand.”
“When I felt lonely, you were always by my side.”
“When you laugh, my heart grows warm.”
Strange. Japanese isn’t his language. But when he writes in Japanese, he can be honest.
Probably because it’s the language they learned together.
Just then there was a knock at the door.
“Mihai, are you awake?” It was Ana’s voice.
Mihai quickly closed his notebook and hid it under the futon.
Ana came in with two cups of tea.
“I can’t sleep either. Because tomorrow is already the last day.”
They sat by the window and drank their tea. Outside was the quiet Hiroshima night.
“Mihai, what was the best thing about this trip?”
“When I wafted the smoke over my head in Asakusa. When the deer ate my map. When Mrs Fumiko cried and laughed…”
“They were all wonderful. But the best…”
“…Was that you were there with me.”
Ana didn’t say anything. But her face went a little red.
Mihai’s heart was pounding. He thought that now was the moment.
But the ring was at the bottom of his bag. And the bag was in the corner of the room.
Getting up now, opening the bag and searching for the box… would be a bit strange.
“Shall we go to Miyajima once more tomorrow?” said Mihai.
“What? You want to let the deer eat your map again?”
“No! I want to see the torii gate at sunset. Because Haruka said that’s when it’s most beautiful.”
After Ana had gone back to her room, Mihai opened his notebook again.
And he wrote the last line.
“I want to be with you for the rest of my life.”
Outside the window, the moon shone quietly.
The next morning, Mihai sent Kenji a message.
“Kenji, this evening, at Miyajima, I’m going to tell Ana.”
The answer came straight away. “Go for it! And make sure the deer doesn’t eat the ring!”
Mihai laughed. But his hands were trembling a little.
He took the little box out of his bag and put it in his pocket. This time he definitely wouldn’t forget it.
Outside the window, morning was beginning in Hiroshima. Today would definitely be a good day.
